question: Is there a relationship between rheumatoid arthritis and periodontal disease?
answer: Among 1,412 individuals attending the University of Queensland's School of Dentistry, patients referred for advanced periodontal care had a significantly higher prevalence of self-reported rheumatoid arthritis (3.95%) than patients not referred for periodontal treatment (0.66%) and than the prevalence reported in the general population (1%) [PMID:10783841]. Of the referred patients who reported rheumatoid arthritis, 62.5% had advanced forms of periodontal disease [PMID:10783841]. This association rests on a cross-sectional analysis of a self-reported health questionnaire and dental records, with rheumatoid arthritis determined by self-report and medication assessment and periodontal disease assessed from existing oral radiographs, so the design cannot establish that periodontal treatment or disease status causes or prevents rheumatoid arthritis [PMID:10783841].

question: Can medical students contribute to quality assurance programmes in day surgery?
answer: Yes — the cited study indicates that senior medical students can contribute to quality assurance (QA) in day surgery: 59 final-year medical students followed allocated patients with common surgical conditions through all phases of the day surgery process, recording each case in a log book and presenting their cases at weekly Problem Based Learning tutorials [PMID:10354335]. Student contribution to QA was evaluated by an audit of student log books and a review of tutorial records covering the 1996 and 1997 academic years [PMID:10354335]. The students followed 621 cases, representing a sampling of 14. 1% day surgery cases [PMID:10354335]. Problems the students highlighted fell into the categories of inappropriate patient and procedure selection, inadequate pain management, discharge, communication and resource issues [PMID:10354335]. The students made recommendations that included multilingual videotapes and patient information sheets for non-English speaking patients, avoiding bilateral surgical procedures, and improved links with local medical officers; they also developed new guidelines and protocols [PMID:10354335].

question: Is delayed gastric emptying following pancreaticoduodenectomy related to pylorus preservation?
answer: Delayed gastric emptying (DGE) is the most frequent postoperative complication after pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy (PPPD), and among 51 patients who underwent PPPD between August 1994 and November 1997 the overall incidence of DGE was 12% (n=6) [PMID:10473855]. In the 36 patients (71%) who had no postoperative complications other than DGE, DGE was seen in only one patient (3%), whereas in the second group of 15 patients in whom postoperative complications other than DGE occurred, five patients (30%) exhibited DGE (P=0.002) [PMID:10473855]. The retrieved study was a prospective, non-randomized study designed to determine whether the incidence of DGE could be reduced by modifying the reconstructive anatomy from a retrocolic to an antecolic duodenojejunostomy; it therefore compared antecolic versus retrocolic reconstruction rather than pylorus-preserving versus pylorus-resecting pancreaticoduodenectomy, and cannot establish whether DGE is related to pylorus preservation [PMID:10473855]. The retrieved evidence does not establish: DGE incidence is related to pylorus preservation, i.e., a comparison of DGE between pylorus-preserving and pylorus-resecting (classical) pancreaticoduodenectomy.

question: Is endothelin-1 an aggravating factor in the development of acute pancreatitis?
answer: Yes — in a rat model, endothelin-1 acts as an aggravating factor in the development of acute pancreatitis: cerulein-induced edematous pancreatitis transformed into hemorrhagic pancreatitis when endothelin-1 was administered [PMID:11601252]. In that rat model, acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis was induced in all rats treated with cerulein plus restraint water-immersion stress, and the pancreatic hemorrhage score in this group was 2.4 +/- 0.2 [PMID:11601252]. In rats pretreated with the ETA receptor antagonist BQ123, the pancreatic hemorrhage score fell to 1.0 +/- 0.0, pancreas wet weight and serum amylase activity were significantly reduced, histologic alterations in the pancreas lightened, and local pancreatic blood flow improved without affecting systemic blood pressure [PMID:11601252].

question: Is year of radical prostatectomy a predictor of outcome in prostate cancer?
answer: Yes — in a multi-center radical prostatectomy cohort, the year of surgery predicted treatment outcome on preoperative multivariate analysis (p = 0.006) but not on postoperative analysis (p = 0.130) [PMID:14713788]. The association between radical prostatectomy year and outcome was examined in 6,556 patients from 7 centers who underwent surgery between 1985 and 2000, using preoperative and pathological features and separate Cox multivariate regression analyses for preoperative and postoperative factors [PMID:14713788]. Patient outcome in that cohort steadily improved with surgery through the mid 1990s and then appeared to level off [PMID:14713788]. The variables analyzed alongside radical prostatectomy year included clinical stage, pretreatment prostate specific antigen, biopsy and RP Gleason sum, margin status, level of extracapsular extension, seminal vesicle status, lymph node status, neoadjuvant hormones and adjuvant therapy; median followup was 23 months (maximum 166) [PMID:14713788].

question: Do inhaled corticosteroids affect perception of dyspnea during bronchoconstriction in asthma?
answer: Some of the disagreements on the perception of dyspnea (PD) during bronchoconstriction in asthma patients could depend on the interrelationships among the following: (1) the influence of baseline airflow obstruction on the patient's ability to detect any further increase in airway resistance; (2) the effect of eosinophilic inflammation on the airway; (3) bronchial hyperresponsiveness (BHR); and (4) the effect of inhaled corticosteroids (ICSs) [PMID:11555508]. In this study, 100 asthma patients were divided into four groups: patients with obstruction who were either ICS-naive (group I) or treated with ICSs (group II), and nonobstructed patients who were either ICS-naive (group III) or treated with ICSs (group IV); PD on the visual analog scale (VAS) was assessed during a methacholine-induced FEV(1) decrease and quantified as the VAS slope and score at an FEV(1) decrease of 5 to 20% [PMID:11555508]. For a 5 to 20% fall in FEV(1) from the lowest point after saline solution induction, VAS score was lowest in group II (obstructed, ICS-treated), slightly higher in group I (obstructed, ICS-naive), slightly higher still in group IV (nonobstructed, ICS-treated), and the highest in group III (nonobstructed, ICS-naive) [PMID:11555508]. Factor analysis yielded four factors that accounted for 70% of the variance in the data: ICS, eosinophil counts, FEV(1) and PC(20) loaded on separated factors, with PD loading on the same factors as PC(20) [PMID:11555508]. The post hoc analysis carried out dividing the patients into ICS-treated and ICS-naive showed that in the former group eosinophil counts and BHR proved to be factors negatively associated with PD, while in the latter group eosinophil counts were positively associated with PD; in patients with obstruction who were treated with ICSs, eosinophil counts related to PD negatively [PMID:11555508]. The comparison of ICS-treated and ICS-naive patients is an observational between-group contrast rather than an intervention in which ICS treatment was assigned, so the observed group differences in perceived dyspnea do not establish the effect of starting or stopping ICSs on perception of dyspnea during bronchoconstriction [PMID:11555508].

question: Is extended aortic replacement in acute type A dissection justifiable?
answer: The cited evidence is mixed and does not establish that extended aortic replacement in acute type A dissection improves clinical outcomes, because the main comparative data come from a retrospective review of aortic arch replacement for type A dissection involving the arch (stented elephant trunk=291, conventional surgical repair=120) rather than a randomized comparison of extended versus limited replacement [PMID:21339481]. Excluding 14 cases of subtotal or total aortic replacement, 411 of 544 patients with type A dissection (stented elephant trunk=291, conventional surgical repair=120) underwent aortic arch replacement between January 2003 and September 2008; in-hospital mortality was 3.09% (9 of 291) for stented repairs (acute 4.73%, 7 of 148; chronic 1.40%, 2 of 143) and 5.00% (6 of 120) for conventional repairs (acute 6.06%, 4 of 66; chronic 3.70%, 2 of 54) [PMID:21339481]. Obliteration of the false lumen around the stented elephant trunk occurred in 94.2% (130 of 138) of patients with acute dissection and in 92.0% (126 of 137) of patients with chronic dissection [PMID:21339481]. Secondary intervention during follow-up was 2.34% (5 of 214) for acute dissection (stented=1 and conventional=4; P=0.031) and 3.05% (6 of 197) for chronic dissection (stented=4 and conventional=2; P=0.661) [PMID:21339481]. Spinal cord injury was 2.41% (7 of 291) in the stented group and 0.83% (1 of 120) in the conventional group, and the overall prevalence of stroke was 1.95% (8 of 411) (stented=2.41%, 7 of 291; conventional=0.83%, 1 of 120) [PMID:21339481]. In reported cases of surgery for acute Stanford type A aortic dissection using an elephant trunk, patients postoperatively developed severe haemolytic anaemia because of a folded elephant trunk; in one case the anaemia improved after additional stent grafting into the elephant trunk [PMID:25228241]. Between January 1995 and March 2001, 43 consecutive patients underwent operations for acute aortic dissection; complete replacement of all dissected tissue could be achieved in 21 patients (group 1), replacement of all the dissected tissue was not possible in 22 patients (group 2) because the distal extent of the dissection was beyond the aortic arch, and 15 patients underwent aortic arch replacement with additional reconstruction of supra-aortic vessels in 3 patients [PMID:12607666]. Because the main comparative report is a retrospective review of aortic arch replacement for type A dissection involving the arch, it cannot establish that extending aortic replacement improves clinical outcomes over a more limited procedure [PMID:21339481].

An 83-yr-old female with an acute type A aortic dissection underwent emergent surgical repair. Proximal extension of the dissection necessitated prolonged cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) and hypothermic circulatory arrest. Despite this, perioperative hemostatis was adequate. Recombinant factor VIIa 90 microg x kg(-1) i.v. was administered post-CPB. The patient had an uneventful postoperative course, and was discharged home neurologically intact.

Two cases of haemolytic anaemia after aortic surgery using the elephant trunk technique were identified from 2011 to 2013. A 64-year-old man, who underwent graft replacement of the ascending aorta for acute Stanford type A aortic dissection, presented with enlargement of the chronic dissection of the descending aorta and moderate aortic regurgitation. A two-stage surgery was scheduled. Total arch replacement with an elephant trunk in the true lumen and concomitant aortic valve replacement were performed. Postoperatively, he developed severe haemolytic anaemia because of the folded elephant trunk. The anaemia improved after the second surgery, including graft replacement of the descending aorta. Similarly, a 61-year-old man, who underwent total arch replacement for acute Stanford type A aortic dissection, presented with enlargement of the chronic dissection of the descending aorta. Graft replacement of the descending aorta with an elephant trunk inserted into the true lumen was performed. The patient postoperatively developed haemolytic anaemia because of the folded elephant trunk, which improved after additional stent grafting into the elephant trunk.

Between January 1995 and March 2001, 43 consecutive patients underwent operations for acute aortic dissection. In all patients the distal repair was performed under circulatory arrest without the use of an aortic cross-clamp. Fifteen patients underwent aortic arch replacement with additional reconstruction of supra-aortic vessels in 3 patients. Complete replacement of all dissected tissue could be achieved in 21 patients (group 1). Because of the distal extent of the dissection beyond the aortic arch, replacement of all the dissected tissue was not possible in 22 patients (group 2).

Excluding 14 cases of subtotal or total aortic replacement, 411 of 544 patients with type A dissection (stented elephant trunk=291, conventional surgical repair=120) underwent aortic arch replacement between January 2003 and September 2008. In-hospital mortality was 3.09% (9 of 291) for stented (acute=4.73%, 7 of 148; chronic=1.40%, 2 of 143) and 5.00% (6 of 120) for conventional repairs (acute=6.06%, 4 of 66; chronic=3.70%, 2 of 54). Spinal cord injury was 2.41% (7 of 291) in the stented and 0.83% (1 of 120) in the conventional group. The overall prevalence of stroke was 1.95% (8 of 411) (stented=2.41%, 7 of 291; conventional=0.83, 1 of 120). Secondary intervention was 2.34% (5 of 214) for acute dissection (stented=1 and conventional=4; P=0.031) and 3.05% (6 of 197) for chronic dissection (stented=4 and conventional=2; P=0.661) during follow-up. Obliteration of the false lumen around the stented elephant trunk occurred in 94.2% (130 of 138) of patients with acute dissection and in 92.0% (126 of 137) of patients with chronic dissection.

Appropriate surgical management of type A dissection is a critical factor for achieving satisfactory outcome, but the choice of optimal procedure is controversial. We retrospectively reviewed our experience with aortic arch replacement for type A dissection involving the arch.

question: Is half-dose contrast-enhanced three-dimensional MR angiography sufficient for the abdominal aorta and pelvis?
answer: Half-dose contrast-enhanced three-dimensional MR angiography was found to be sufficient for depicting the abdominal aorta and its iliac (pelvic) branches, because overall image quality did not differ significantly among the four contrast groups [PMID:14745753]. In the randomized study, 72 consecutive patients were assigned to one of four groups that received gadolinium chelate differing in concentration (original or diluted to 50%), total amount (single or half-dose) and injection rate (1 or 0.5 mL/second) [PMID:14745753]. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) were calculated for the abdominal aorta and the common and external iliac arteries, and two blinded readers rated the respective image qualities [PMID:14745753]. SNR and CNR of the abdominal aorta and the common iliac artery in the 0.5 mL/second groups were statistically significantly lower than those in the 1 mL/second groups, while the differences in overall image quality across the four groups were not statistically significant [PMID:14745753].

chunks.text: To evaluate the usefulness of half-dose contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance (MR) angiography for depicting the abdominal aorta and its major branches.

A total of 72 consecutive patients were randomly assigned to one of four groups that underwent MR angiography after receiving different concentrations (original or diluted to 50%) and total amounts (single or half-dose) of gadolinium chelate injected at different rates (1 or 0.5 mL/second). The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of the abdominal aorta and of the common and external iliac arteries were calculated, and two blinded readers rated the respective image qualities.

The SNR and CNR of the abdominal aorta and the common iliac artery in the 0.5 mL/second groups were statistically significantly lower than those in the 1 mL/second groups. The differences in overall image quality across the four groups were not statistically significant.

With institutional review board approval and informed consent, 57 patients with early RA underwent 3-T magnetic resonance (MR) imaging with two different doses of contrast media. The contrast enhancement was measured in inflamed synovial tissue at half dose (0.05 mmol per kilogram of body weight) and at full dose (0.1 mmol/kg) by using T1-weighted sequences with fat saturation. The differences and the correlation of signal intensities (SIs) at half- and full-dose sequences were compared by using the paired t test and Pearson correlations. Image quality, Rheumatoid Arthritis MRI Score (RAMRIS), and tenosynovitis score on half- and full-dose images were compared by two observers using the Wilcoxon test. Interrater agreement was assessed by using κ statistics.

MR angiography (MRA) is increasingly used as a noninvasive imaging technique for the follow-up of coiled intracranial aneurysms. However, the need for contrast enhancement has not yet been elucidated. We compared 3D time-of-flight MRA (TOF-MRA) and contrast-enhanced MRA (CE-MRA) at 3T with catheter angiography.

This HIPAA-compliant study was exempt from institutional review board approval; informed patient consent was waived. Eighty-five patients (66 men, 19 women; mean age, 66 years; range, 45-81 years) underwent 110 multidetector CT examinations after endovascular repair of abdominal aortic aneurysms. Nonenhanced CT images were obtained. Intravenous contrast material was then injected at 4 mL/sec, and arterial and venous phase (60 seconds) CT images were obtained. The nonenhanced and venous phase images were evaluated to determine if an endoleak was present. Subsequently, arterial phase images were analyzed. The effective dose was calculated. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals as indicators of how often arterial phase imaging would contribute to the diagnosis of endoleak were determined.

chunks.text: There is a paucity of literature surrounding the safety and feasibility of laparoscopic repair for acutely incarcerated abdominal hernias. The objective of this study was to compare the 30-day morbidity and mortality between laparoscopic and open repairs of incarcerated abdominal hernias.

A retrospective cohort study was conducted using data from the National Surgery Quality Improvement Program from 2005 to 2012. The study population was selected using ICD-9 diagnostic codes describing abdominal hernias with obstruction, but without gangrene. Cases with documented bowel resection were excluded. Group classification was based on CPT coding. Study outcomes included the 30-day major complication, reoperation and mortality rates. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to adjust for confounding for all study outcomes.

A total of 2688 and 15,562 patients were in the laparoscopic and open group, respectively. After adjustment for clinically relevant confounders, laparoscopic surgery was associated with a significantly lower 30-day infectious (OR 0.36, p < 0.001, 95 % CI 0.23-0.56) and serious complication rates (OR 0.66, p < 0.001, 95 % CI 0.55-0.80). However, there was no statistical difference with respect to the 30-day reoperation (OR 0.81, p = 0.28, 95 % CI 0.56-1.18) or mortality rates (OR 0.94, p = 0.80, 95 % CI 0.58-1.53).

Elective inguinal hernia repair as a day case is a safe and suitable procedure, with well-recognized feasibility. The increasing number of elderly patients requiring inguinal hernia repair leads clinicians to admit a growing number of outpatients. The aim of the current study was to analyze the outcomes (feasibility and safety) of day case treatment in elderly patients.

Laparoscopy has rapidly emerged as the preferred surgical approach to a number of different diseases because it allows for a correct diagnosis and proper treatment. It seems to be moving toward the use of mini-instruments (5 mm or less in diameter). The aim of this paper is to illustrate retrospectively the results of an initial experience of minilaparoscopic transabdominal preperitoneal (miniTAPP) repair of groin hernia defects performed at two institutions.

Sixteen male infants with large inguinal hernias (hernia extending to the bottom of the scrotum and the diameter of the open internal ring>2 cm on laparoscopy) underwent laparoscopic hernia repair. Diagnostic laparoscopy was performed under general anesthesia with a telescopic port at the umbilicus. If the internal ring was open, two working ports were introduced pararectally on either side. An open internal ring was considered an indication for hernia repair. The needle, carrying 3-0 nylon nonabsorbable sutures, was introduced through the groin skin at the internal inguinal ring and the internal ring was closed by taking continuous sutures to approximate the edges of the ring. The needle was then taken out through the entry point and the knot was tied extracorporeally and buried in the subcutaneous tissue. In 4 patients in the initial part of the study, intracorporeal (knot tied internally) suturing was done to close the internal ring. A contralateral repair was done if the internal ring was open.

There were 1164 patients who underwent a unilateral inguinal hernia repair during the 10-year study period, and laparoscopy was used in 1010 patients. There were no intraoperative complications from the laparoscopy. In the group who underwent laparoscopy, the mean age was 4.0±3.6 years old, and 88% were male. At laparoscopic exploration, 315 (31%) patients were found to have a CPPV. There were 10 patients (1.0%) who developed a surgical site infection. question: Can normal knee kinematics be restored with unicompartmental knee replacement?
answer: In an in vivo motion-capture study of stair ascent, patients with medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (MED-UKA, 17 participants) or lateral unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (LAT-UKA, nine participants), all with nondiseased contralateral limbs, showed no clinically meaningful mean interlimb differences in temporal gait or knee angular kinematics in either group, indicating that mean kinematics were symmetrical between the operated and nonoperated limbs [PMID:22895693]. Interlimb symmetry was classified by comparing observed interlimb differences against clinically meaningful thresholds set at 5% of stride time for temporal variables and 5° for angular variables, and approximately half of the participants in each UKA group displayed asymmetry favoring the operative or nonoperative limb with similar frequency [PMID:22895693]. For each limb, participants walked up four stairs for five trials while a motion-capture system obtained reflective marker locations, with temporal events determined from force platform signals; minimum postoperative follow-up was 6 months (median, 24 months; range, 6-53 months) [PMID:22895693]. In the cadaveric study it was hypothesized that knee kinematics after unicompartmental replacement may be unchanged, because in unicompartmental replacement the other compartments and knee ligaments are largely untouched [PMID:15687156]. Six human cadaver knees were tested before implantation, after implantation with a bicruciate-retaining unicompartmental knee prosthesis, and after implantation with a posterior cruciate-retaining tricompartmental knee prosthesis; the unicompartmental prosthesis was initially implanted and then revised to a total condylar knee replacement [PMID:15687156]. Knee kinematics were measured with use of an electromagnetic tracking device while the knee was put through dynamic simulated stair-climbing under peak flexion moments of approximately 40 N-m [PMID:15687156]. chunks.text: Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) has long been a treatment option for patients with disease limited primarily to one compartment with small, correctable deformities. However, some surgeons presume that normal kinematics of a lateral compartment UKA are difficult to achieve. Furthermore, it is unclear whether UKA restores normal knee kinematics and interlimb symmetry.QUESTIONS/

We determined knee kinematics exhibited during stair ascent by patients with medial- (MED-UKA) or lateral-UKA (LAT-UKA) and if the knee kinematics of the operated and nonoperated limbs were symmetrical.

Participants were 17 individuals with MED-UKA and nine with LAT-UKA, all with nondiseased contralateral limbs. For each limb, participants walked up four stairs for five trials while a motion-capture system obtained reflective marker locations. Temporal events were determined by force platform signals. Interlimb symmetry was classified for temporal gait and knee angular kinematics by comparing observed interlimb differences with clinically meaningful differences set at 5% of stride time for temporal variables and 5° for angular variables. The minimum postoperative followup was 6 months (median, 24 months; range, 6-53 months).

Neither group demonstrated clinically meaningful mean interlimb differences. However, approximately half of participants of each UKA group displayed asymmetry favoring the operative or nonoperative limb with similar frequency.

Unicompartmental replacement can be an alternative to tibial osteotomy in younger, active patients with unicompartmental knee disease. In unicompartmental replacement, the other compartments and knee ligaments are largely untouched. Therefore, it was hypothesized that the knee kinematics after unicompartmental replacement may also be unchanged. To test this hypothesis, knee kinematics and quadriceps tension were recorded before and after replacement with a unicompartmental design and then with a tricompartmental design.

Six human cadaver knees were tested before implantation, after implantation with a bicruciate-retaining unicompartmental knee prosthesis, and after implantation with a posterior cruciate-retaining tricompartmental knee prosthesis. The unicompartmental prosthesis was initially implanted, and it was then revised to a total condylar knee replacement. The knee kinematics were measured with use of an electromagnetic tracking device while the knee was put through dynamic simulated stair-climbing under peak flexion moments of approximately 40 N-m. Quadriceps tension was also measured for all three conditions.

Bicompartmental knee arthroplasty features bone and ligament sparing as unicompartmental knee arthroplasty and is presumably better in the recovery of muscle strength and function compared to total knee arthroplasty (TKA) though not previously reported in the literature. The aim of the study was to compare isokinetic knee muscle strength and physical performance in patients who underwent either bicompartmental knee arthroplasty or TKA.

question: Women with synchronous primary cancers of the endometrium and ovary: do they have Lynch syndrome?
answer: Among women with synchronous primary cancers of the endometrium and ovary, a minority have findings indicating Lynch syndrome (HNPCC): of 102 women identified between 1989 and 2004, two met Amsterdam criteria for HNPCC and five additional patients, all in the medium-risk family-history group, had molecular findings consistent with a germline mutation of either MSH2 or MLH1 [PMID:16361634]. None of the low-risk patients in that series had molecular results consistent with a germline mutation [PMID:16361634]. In this study, protein expression for MSH2, MSH6 and MLH1 was evaluated by immunohistochemistry, and microsatellite instability and MLH1 promoter methylation analyses were performed on a subset of cases; tumor blocks were available for analysis in 59 of the 102 identified patients [PMID:16361634].

chunks.text: Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer; HNPCC) is an autosomal-dominant cancer predisposition syndrome that increases risk for multiple cancers, including colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancer. Revised Bethesda Criteria recommend that patients with two HNPCC-associated cancers undergo molecular evaluation to determine whether they have a mismatch repair (MMR) defect associated with HNPCC. The purpose of our study was to determine the likelihood of MMR defects (MSH2, MSH6, MLH1) in women with synchronous endometrial and ovarian cancer.

Between 1989 and 2004, 102 women with synchronous endometrial and ovarian cancers were identified; 59 patients had tumor blocks available for analysis. Patients were divided into risk groups based on family history: high (met Amsterdam criteria), medium (personal history or first-degree relative with an HNPCC-associated cancer), and low (all others). Protein expression for MSH2, MSH6, and MLH1 was evaluated by immunohistochemistry. Microsatellite instability and MLH1 promoter methylation analyses were performed on a subset of cases.

Median age was 50 years. Two patients met Amsterdam criteria for HNPCC. Five additional patients, all medium-risk, had molecular findings consistent with a germline mutation of either MSH2 or MLH1. None of the low-risk patients had molecular results consistent with a germline mutation.

Evidence is accumulating supporting the use of screening for colorectal cancer. Patients at higher risk for colorectal cancer are more likely to benefit from screening. Women with breast, endometrial, or ovarian cancer are often classified as at high risk for subsequent colorectal cancer, and are urged to undergo screening, but the basis for this is uncertain.

Between January 2006 and September 2013, women who underwent MIS for endometrial, cervical or ovarian cancer at a single institution were included. Data on patient demographics, diagnosis, comorbidities, perioperative characteristics, use of thromboprophylaxis, and diagnosis of VTE were collected retrospectively.

5346 patients were eligible for the study and divided into three groups: solitary, synchronous and metachronous CRC. The overall prevalence of the synchronous CRC was 2.2% and the 10-year cumulative incidence of metachronous cancer was 0.84%. 29 (64%) metachronous cancers were diagnosed within 3 years of the index cancer and the mean time interval was 3.2 years. Male gender and presence of associated adenoma were significant risk factors for both synchronous and metachronous CRC. Synchronous and metachronous CRC patients shared similar clinicopathological features except that the former were older than the latter by 3.7 years. The five-year survival rates were not different among the three groups.

question: Does rural or urban residence make a difference to neonatal outcome in premature birth?
answer: Yes — rural residence was associated with worse neonatal outcome in very premature birth: among 1879 rural and 6775 urban infants born at <32 weeks' gestation in 1992-2002 and admitted to all 10 neonatal intensive care units in New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory, infants of rural maternal residence had a higher case-mix adjusted mortality than urban infants (adjusted odds ratio 1.26, 95% confidence interval 1.07 to 1.48, p = 0.005) [PMID:16428354]. The higher mortality trend for rural infants was consistently seen in all subgroups and was significant for the tertiary hospital-born population and for the 30-31 weeks gestation subgroup, and regional birth data in this gestational age range also showed a higher stillbirth rate among rural infants (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.32, p<0.001) [PMID:16428354]. This was an observational comparison of infants grouped by location of maternal residence, so the reported rural-urban mortality difference cannot establish that changing residence or the referral and transport system would itself alter neonatal outcomes [PMID:16428354].

"Rural" or "urban" status was based on the location of maternal residence. This trend was consistently seen in all subgroups and significantly for the tertiary hospital born population and the 30-31 weeks gestation subgroup. Regional birth data in this gestational age range also showed a higher stillbirth rate among rural infants (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.32, p<0.001).

Observations on a cohort of neonates in the preintervention year of the field trial of home-based neonatal care (HBNC) in rural Gadchiroli, India, showed that preterm birth and low birth weight (LBW),<2500 g, constituted the most important risk factors. Owing to a limited access to hospital care, most neonates were managed at home in the subsequent intervention years. The objective of this paper is to evaluate the feasibility and effectiveness of managing LBW and preterm neonates in home setting.

The response rate from midwives in rural settings was considerably higher (85%) than from midwives in the urban areas (60%). Although the proportion of midwives who reported that they were competent was broadly similar in the two groups, there were some significant differences regarding specific competencies. Midwives in the rural group were more likely to report competence for breech delivery (p = 0.001), while more urban midwives reported competence in skills such as intravenous fluid replacement (p<0.001) and initial and discharge examination of the newborn (p<0.001). Both groups reported facing barriers to continuing professional development; however, more of the rural group had attended an educational event within the last month (p<0.001). Lack of time was a greater barrier for urban midwives (p = 0.02), whereas distance to training was greater for rural midwives (p = 0.009). Lack of motivation or interest was significantly higher in urban units (p = 0.006).

question: Counter sampling combined with medical provider education: do they alter prescribing behavior?
answer: Counter sampling combined with pharmacist education altered prescribing behavior only partially: in a pretest-posttest controlled study at two rural private clinics, COX-2 NSAID prescribing relative to total NSAIDs fell significantly in the intervention group, but prescribing of focus-nonsedating antihistamines and proton pump inhibitors continued to rise significantly rather than declining [PMID:17076590]. Eight medical providers at the clinic receiving the active intervention were given education from pharmacists on lower-cost alternatives to expensive focus medications plus counter samples and patient sample handouts to dispense at their discretion; seven providers at the control clinic received no intervention [PMID:17076590]. The prescribing behavior of the active intervention and control groups differed significantly at baseline in all three focus medication categories, which the authors state indicated that results should be interpreted as changes across the two study years within each group rather than as comparisons between the two groups [PMID:17076590]. Following active intervention, the intervention group significantly decreased COX-2 NSAID prescriptions relative to total NSAID prescriptions, from 38.9% in year 1 to 23.7% in year 2 (P<0.05), whereas the control site showed a nonstatistically significant decrease over the same two periods, from 67.5% to 62% (P>0.05) [PMID:17076590]. Education and counter sampling did not stop medical providers in the intervention group from significantly increasing total yearly prescriptions for antihistamines and acid-relief medications consisting of focus-nonsedating antihistamines (86.7% versus 93.1%, P<0.05) and proton pump inhibitors (68.9% versus 86.2%, P<0.05) [PMID:17076590]. Statistically significant increases in the prescribing of focus-nonsedating antihistamines (77.9% versus 98.3%, P<0.05) and proton pump inhibitors (77.5% versus 91.4%, P<0.05) were also observed in the control group over the same period [PMID:17076590].

question: Recurrent spontaneous abortion and skewed X-inactivation: is there an association?
answer: The cited evidence indicates no clear association between recurrent spontaneous abortion and skewed X-inactivation: the rate of extreme skewing (90% or greater) in the recurrent spontaneous abortion population was 8.6% and was not statistically different from any of the other groups, except the Primiparous group (1.0%, P<.01) [PMID:17403428]. The study was designed to determine whether there is an association between skewed X-inactivation and recurrent spontaneous abortion in a large, well-defined sample of women with recurrent loss, and X-chromosome inactivation patterns were compared across 5 groups of women [PMID:17403428]. Group 1 (recurrent spontaneous abortion) consisted of 357 women with 2 or more spontaneous losses; group 2 (infertility) comprised 349 subjects from infertility practices recruited at the time of a positive serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin; group 3 (spontaneous abortion) comprised 81 women recruited at the time of an ultrasound diagnosis of an embryonic demise or an anembryonic gestation; the Primiparous group included 114 women in their first pregnancy; and the Multiparous group consisted of 79 women with 2 or more pregnancies but without pregnancy loss [PMID:17403428]. Within the recurrent loss population, the incidence of X-inactivation skewing of 90% or greater was no different whether there had been at least 1 live birth (9.9%) or no previous live births and at least 3 losses (5.6%, P>.05) [PMID:17403428]. As a related reported observation, subjects with extreme skewing of 90% or greater had a mean age 2 years older than those without extreme skewing (P<.05) [PMID:17403428].

question: Is tumour expression of VEGF associated with venous invasion and survival in pT3 renal cell carcinoma?
answer: Tumour VEGF expression was not significantly associated with venous invasion in pT3 renal cell carcinoma: when 78 patients with a pT3a or pT3b tumour without vena cava invasion or a pT3b tumour with vena cava invasion were compared for age, gender, Fuhrman grade and immunohistochemical expression of VEGF, only tumour size appeared to be significantly different between the 3 groups [PMID:17489316]. Tumour VEGF expression was significantly associated with survival in pT3 renal cell carcinoma: after the variables were submitted to univariate and multivariate analysis, invasion of the perirenal fat, lymph node involvement, distant metastases and VEGF expression were significantly associated with survival on univariate analysis (p<0.01), and on multivariate analysis lymph node involvement, distant metastases and VEGF expression (OR 6.07) were identified as independent predictive factors of survival [PMID:17489316].

question: Cholestasis associated with small bowel atresia: do we always need to investigate?
answer: In a retrospective review of patients with small bowel atresia (SBA) treated between 1996 and 2005, care was withdrawn for 2 patients before repair, leaving 53 patients whose atresia was duodenal in 18, jejunoileal in 32 and multiple in 3; of these 53, 24 (45%) developed cholestasis postoperatively, defined as direct/total bilirubin greater than 20% [PMID:17502203]. All 4 patients with short bowel and 6 of 10 patients (60%) whose enteral feeding was delayed more than 14 days postoperatively had cholestasis; no deaths were related to isolated cholestasis or cirrhosis, and cholestasis resolved spontaneously in all the survivors [PMID:17502203]. Among patients with SBA-associated cholestasis, 10 patients (36%) proceeded with in-depth evaluations for cholestasis and 8 (28%) underwent liver biopsy, yet no patient had biliary atresia, and cholestasis resolved spontaneously in all the survivors [PMID:17502203].

Ten patients (36%) proceeded with in-depth evaluations for cholestasis, with 8 (28%) undergoing liver biopsy. No patient had biliary atresia. No deaths were related to isolated cholestasis/cirrhosis. question: Is being small for gestational age a risk factor for retinopathy of prematurity?
answer: In a prospective cohort of preterm infants with birth weight ≤1,500 g and gestational age ≤32 weeks, SGA status was not significantly associated with development of any evolutive stage ROP: ROP occurred in 36 SGA infants (24.7%) versus 66 AGA infants (33.2%) (p = 0.111). Of the 345 patients examined, 199 were in the AGA group and 146 in the SGA group, and mean birth weight and gestational age for the whole cohort were 1,128.12 g (±239.9) and 29.7 weeks (±1.9), respectively [PMID:19198736]. SGA status was likewise not significantly associated with severe ROP requiring treatment: severe ROP occurred in nine SGA infants (6.2%) versus 15 AGA infants (7.5%) (p = 0.779), while the overall prevalence of any stage ROP and of severe ROP needing treatment in the cohort was 29.6% and 7.0%, respectively [PMID:19198736]. In the adjusted logistic regression analysis, weight gain from birth to the sixth week of life and need for blood transfusions were significant risk factors for ROP in both the SGA and AGA groups, whereas SGA status itself was not reported as a significant independent risk factor [PMID:19198736].

question: Aromatase inhibitor-related musculoskeletal symptoms: is preventing osteoporosis the key to eliminating these symptoms?
answer: Patients receiving aromatase inhibitors (AIs) for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer are reported to have a higher incidence of musculoskeletal symptoms and bone fractures, although the mechanism and risk factors for this correlation were described as not well studied [PMID:19299238]. The evidence comes from a chart review of 856 patients with hormone receptor-positive nonmetastatic breast cancer seen at one institution between January 1999 and October 2007, of whom 316 met the inclusion criteria of AI treatment for 3 months or more and availability of a dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan during that treatment; arthralgia, generalized bone pain and/or myalgia, bone fracture after starting AIs, any tamoxifen treatment, and calcium/bisphosphonate therapy were recorded [PMID:19299238]. question: Can you deliver accurate tidal volume by manual resuscitator?
answer: One of the problems with manual resuscitators is the difficulty in achieving accurate volume delivery, and the volume delivered to the patient varies by the physical characteristics of the person and the method used [PMID:18843057]. In this study, 114 individuals trained in basic life support and bag-valve-mask ventilation participated; ventilation was delivered with a manual resuscitator connected to a microspirometer and volumes were measured, and subjects completed three procedures: one-handed, two-handed and two-handed half-compression [PMID:18843057]. The mean (standard deviation) volumes for the one-handed method were 592.84 ml (SD 117.39), two-handed 644.24 ml (SD 144.7) and two-handed half-compression 458.31 ml (SD 120.91) (p<0.01), and tidal volume delivered by two hands was significantly greater than that delivered by one hand (r = 0.398, p<0.01) [PMID:18843057]. The physical aspects including hand size, volume and grip power had no correlation with the volume delivered, and there were slight increases in tidal volume with education and practice, but correlation was weak (r = 0.213, r = 0.281, r = 0.131, p<0.01) [PMID:18843057]. the authors enrolled 50 providers from a large, busy, urban fire-based EMS agency with 14.96 (SD = 9.92) mean years of experience; only 1.5% of all breaths delivered with the pediatric BVM during the ventilation scenarios were below the recommended tidal volume, and a greater percentage of breaths delivered in the recommended range occurred when the pediatric BVM was used (17.5% vs 5.1%, p<0.001) [PMID:27690714]. Median volumes for each scenario were 570.5mL, 664.0mL, 663.0mL for the pediatric BMV and 796.0mL, 994.5mL, 981.5mL for the adult BVM, and in all three categories of airway devices, the pediatric BVM provided lower median tidal volumes (p<0.001) [PMID:27690714].

question: Does telmisartan prevent hepatic fibrosis in rats with alloxan-induced diabetes?
answer: The retrieved evidence does not directly establish whether telmisartan prevents hepatic fibrosis in alloxan-induced diabetic rats, because no collagen deposition or fibrosis scoring outcome is reported; the closest reported findings are that liver sections from telmisartan-treated diabetic rats showed no TGF-beta immunoreactivity, whereas the diabetic control group was strongly immunoreactive to TGF-beta [PMID:19406119]. In this study, 15 adult male rats were divided into a non-diabetic healthy group, an alloxan-induced diabetic control group, and an alloxan-induced diabetic telmisartan group; the healthy and diabetic control groups received saline for 30 days while the treated group received oral telmisartan 10 mg/kg/day for 30 days, after which the rats were sacrificed and the livers evaluated using stereological and histopathological methods [PMID:19406119]. Stereological assessment of the numerical density of hepatocytes showed a significant difference between the alloxan-induced diabetic control group and the diabetic rats treated with telmisartan [PMID:19406119]. Immunohistochemical staining for TGF-beta in liver sections showed no immunoreactivity in the diabetic rats treated with telmisartan, while the diabetic control group was determined to be strongly immunoreactive to TGF-beta [PMID:19406119]. Because the reported hepatic evaluation used stereology and histopathology together with TGF-beta immunohistochemistry rather than a direct fibrosis measure such as collagen deposition or fibrosis scoring, this design cannot establish that telmisartan prevents hepatic fibrosis in alloxan-induced diabetic rats [PMID:19406119]. The retrieved evidence does not establish: Direct hepatic fibrosis outcome.

question: Does elective re-siting of intravenous cannulae decrease peripheral thrombophlebitis?
answer: Yes — elective re-siting of intravenous cannulae every 48 hours decreased peripheral thrombophlebitis (PVT) in a randomized trial in patients receiving intravenous fluids or drugs, where PVT occurred in 100% (21/21) of the control group versus 9.5% (2/21) of the elective re-siting group (p<0.0001) [PMID:19852337]. The trial randomized 42 patients admitted for major abdominal surgery to a control or study group (n = 21 in each); control cannulae were removed only if the site became painful, the cannula was dislodged, or there were signs and symptoms suggestive of PVT (pain, erythema, swelling, excessive warmth or a palpable venous cord), whereas study-group cannulae were changed and re-sited electively every 48 hours, and all patients were examined every 24 hours for PVT signs at the current and previous infusion sites [PMID:19852337]. The severity of PVT was also lower in the elective re-siting study group than in the control group [PMID:19852337]. Day-wise correlation of PVT incidence showed that 82.6% of the episodes occurred on day 3 [PMID:19852337].

question: Do symptoms matter when considering patients for phase I clinical trials?
answer: Yes — in a retrospective chart review of phase I clinical trial participants older than 60 years, older adults with more than 3 symptoms had significantly more hospital admissions, more complications and greater decline in functional status than those with 3 or fewer symptoms, whereas no significant differences were found when the same group was compared by age [PMID:21398266]. Among the 56 phase I clinical trial participants older than 60 years (mean age 67.09 years; 48.21% female), those with >3 symptoms had more admissions (37.5% vs 14.29%; P = .0335), more complications (46.43% vs 16.07%; P = .0026), and greater decline in functional status (24 participants with >3 symptoms vs 8; P = .0173) than participants with ≤3 symptoms [PMID:21398266]. Comparing older adults by age (>65 vs 60-65 years) yielded no significant differences, indicating that symptom burden rather than age distinguished those with worse outcomes in this cohort [PMID:21398266]. Because this evidence comes from a retrospective chart review rather than a prospective or interventional design, it can support an association between symptom burden and adverse outcomes in older phase I trial participants but cannot establish that acting on symptoms changes those outcomes [PMID:21398266].

question: Are there progressive brain changes in schizophrenia?
answer: Yes—a systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of longitudinal region-of-interest volumetric MRI studies found that subjects with schizophrenia showed significantly greater decreases over time in whole brain volume, whole brain gray matter, frontal gray and white matter, parietal white matter, and temporal white matter volume, and larger increases in lateral ventricular volume, than healthy control subjects, indicating progressive brain changes in schizophrenia [PMID:21457946]. That review pooled longitudinal volumetric studies using region-of-interest structural magnetic resonance imaging in patients with schizophrenia and healthy control subjects, obtaining the percentage change in volume between scans for each region of interest and combining data by random effects meta-analysis [PMID:21457946]. Twenty-seven studies were included in the meta-analysis, comprising 928 patients and 867 control subjects across 32 different brain regions of interest, with the time between baseline and follow-up MRI scans ranging from 1 to 10 years [PMID:21457946]. The differences between patients and control subjects in annualized percentage volume change were -0.07% for whole brain volume, -0.59% for whole brain gray matter, -0.32% for frontal white matter, -0.32% for parietal white matter, -0.39% for temporal white matter, and +0.36% for bilateral lateral ventricles [PMID:21457946].

question: Type II supracondylar humerus fractures: can some be treated nonoperatively?
answer: Yes: in a review of clinical and radiographic data from 259 pediatric type II supracondylar humerus fractures enrolled in a prospective registry, 150 fractures (57.9%) were ultimately treated nonoperatively and 109 (42.1%) were treated surgically, indicating that some type II fractures can be managed without surgery [PMID:22955530]. During the course of treatment, 39 of the fractures were found to have unsatisfactory alignment with nonoperative management and were taken for surgery [PMID:22955530]. At final follow-up, outcome measures of change in carrying angle, elbow range of motion, and complications did not show clinically significant differences between the nonoperative and surgical treatment groups [PMID:22955530]. Fractures without rotational deformity or coronal angulation and with a shaft-condylar angle of greater than 15 degrees were more likely to be associated with successful nonsurgical treatment [PMID:22955530]. Patients with isolated extension deformity, but none of the other assessed features, were more likely to complete successful nonoperative management [PMID:22955530]. Because this evidence comes from a review of a prospective registry in which patients treated without surgery were compared with those treated surgically rather than from a randomized comparison, the reported associations between fracture features and successful nonoperative management do not by themselves establish that selecting treatment on those features improves outcomes [PMID:22955530].

question: Does responsibility affect the public's valuation of health care interventions?
answer: The study investigated whether the public value safety-related health care improvements more highly than the same improvements in contexts where the health care system is not responsible [PMID:22867778]. An online survey was conducted to elicit the relative importance placed on preventing harms caused by 1) health care (hospital-acquired infections, drug administration errors, injuries to health care staff), 2) individuals (personal lifestyle choices, sports-related injuries), and 3) nature (genetic disorders) [PMID:22867778]. Direct valuations were obtained from members of the public by using a person trade-off or "matching" method [PMID:22867778]. Participants were asked to choose between two preventative interventions of equal cost and equal health benefit per person for the same number of people, but differing in causation [PMID:22867778]. If participants indicated a preference, their strength of preference was measured by using person trade-off [PMID:22867778]. Participants valued interventions preventing hospital-acquired infections (1.31) more highly than genetic disorders (1.0), although drug errors were valued similarly to genetic disorders (1.07), and interventions to prevent injury to health care staff were given less weight than genetic disorders (0.71) [PMID:22867778]. Less weight was also given to interventions related to lifestyle (0.65) and sports injuries (0.41) [PMID:22867778]. Responses were obtained from 1030 people, reflecting the sociodemographic mix of the UK population [PMID:22867778]. These valuations indicate that causation affected the public's valuation: interventions preventing hospital-acquired infections were valued above genetic disorders, whereas drug errors were valued similarly and staff injuries, lifestyle-related harms, and sports injuries were valued below genetic disorders [PMID:22867778].

question: Should pulp chamber pulpotomy be seen as a permanent treatment?
answer: The retrieved evidence does not support regarding pulp chamber pulpotomy as a permanent treatment, since the only reported outcome data come from a case series of 17 patients followed for just 12 to 24 months, after which 82% of the treated teeth survived without any complementary treatment at 24 months [PMID:22900881]. In that series, 17 patients aged 7 to 54 years (mean 37.2 years) with vital pulps and no clinical evidence of irreversible pulpitis in premolar or molar teeth were treated by pulpotomy and filling with ProRoot MTA, then followed for 12 to 24 months and assessed clinically and radiographically [PMID:22900881]. Survival without any complementary treatment at 24 months was estimated at 82%, and 3 of the 17 treated teeth needed root canal treatment — two for pain control and one for prosthetic reasons [PMID:22900881]. Because the follow-up in this study ended at 24 months, it cannot establish long-term or permanent success of pulp chamber pulpotomy beyond that period [PMID:22900881]. question: Pancreas retransplantation:  a second chance for diabetic patients?
answer: Yes — pancreas retransplantation offers a genuine second chance in this single Lyon/Geneva series: among the 17 patients retransplanted from 1995, second pancreas survival was 71% at 1 year and 59% at 5 years, close to primary graft survival of the whole population (79% and 69% respectively; P=0.5075) and significantly better than those same patients' first pancreas survival (29% at 1 year and 7% at 5 years; P=0.0008), irrespective of the cause of first graft loss [PMID:23222920]. Second graft survival was compared with primary graft survival of the same patients and of the whole population in a series of 569 pancreas transplantations performed in Lyon and Geneva between 1976 and 2008, which included 37 second transplantations, and the same results were observed when all 37 retransplantations were considered [PMID:23222920]. Survival of second simultaneous pancreas and kidney transplantations was better than survival of second pancreas after kidney [PMID:23222920]. Patient survival was excellent, at 89% at 5 years, and pancreas retransplantation had no impact on kidney graft function and survival, which was 100% at 5 years [PMID:23222920]. The study evaluated pancreas retransplantation outcome in type 1 diabetic patients with end-stage renal disease, a population for whom pancreas transplantation is a validated alternative but the management of patients who have lost their primary graft is poorly defined [PMID:23222920].

question: Do provider service networks result in lower expenditures compared with HMOs or primary care case management in Florida's Medicaid program?
answer: Among SSI enrollees in Florida's Medicaid Demonstration, provider service networks (PSNs) lowered per member per month (PMPM) Medicaid expenditures by $7 more than HMOs [PMID:24237112]. Using a difference-in-difference approach comparing enrollee expenditures before and after implementation, the Demonstration was associated with lower increases in PMPM expenditures over time among SSI enrollees ($40) than in the non-Demonstration counties ($186), a comparison made specifically for HMOs and PSNs [PMID:24237112]. As an interpretation of the reported design, the comparison set was Demonstration counties versus non-Demonstration counties, with HMOs versus PSNs compared within the Demonstration, so this evidence does not provide a direct PSN-versus-primary-care-case-management expenditure comparison [PMID:24237112]. The retrieved evidence does not establish: PSN versus primary care case management expenditure comparison.

question: Delayed imaging in routine CT examinations of the abdomen and pelvis: is it worth the additional cost of radiation and time?
answer: In a retrospective evaluation of routine contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT scans from 1000 consecutive patients (912 men, 88 women; average age, 60 years; range, 22-94 years), 42 patients (4.2%) had findings that were further characterized or observed only in the delayed phase, while delayed imaging was of no benefit in the other 958 patients (95.8%) [PMID:24450673]. Most of these findings were incidental and could have been confirmed at noninvasive follow-up imaging such as sonography or unenhanced CT or MRI; the most common were liver hemangioma (n = 12), adrenal adenoma (n = 12), and parapelvic renal cysts (n = 6) [PMID:24450673]. The most important finding was detection of a renal mass in one patient (0.1%), which was seen only on the delayed phase images and was difficult to appreciate in the portal venous phase [PMID:24450673]. Radiation doses for both the portal venous and delayed phases, when available, were analyzed to assess the effect of the delayed phase on overall radiation exposure; use of the delayed phase resulted in a mean 59.5% increase in effective radiation dose [PMID:24450673]. With respect to radiation, delayed phase imaging provided additional diagnostic information in 4.2% of patients and detected a renal mass in 0.1%, but was of no benefit in 95.8% and increased effective radiation dose by a mean of 59.5% [PMID:24450673]. question: Pharmacologic regimens for knee osteoarthritis prevention: can they be cost-effective?
answer: The cost-effectiveness of pharmacologic prophylaxis for knee osteoarthritis was assessed in a validated state-transition simulation model of knee OA, the Osteoarthritis Policy (OAPol) Model, using disease-modifying OA drugs (DMOADs) as prophylaxis for the disease [PMID:24487044]. The base case DMOAD regimen in that model was initiated at age 50 and assumed 40% efficacy in the first year, 5% failure per subsequent year, 0.22% major toxicity, and an annual cost of $1,000 [PMID:24487044]. Whether prophylaxis can be cost-effective is mixed and depends on baseline risk: for the high-risk cohort (obese with a history of knee injury), base case prophylaxis increased quality-adjusted life-years by 0.04 and lifetime costs by $4,600, producing an ICER of $118,000 per QALY gained [PMID:24487044]. Compared with the standard of care, the base case DMOAD yielded ICERs greater than $150,000/QALY in the knee injury only cohort, and was less cost-effective than the standard of care in the obese only and no risk factors cohorts [PMID:24487044]. Regimens priced at $3,000 per year and higher demonstrated ICERs above cost-effectiveness thresholds consistent with current US standards [PMID:24487044].

question: Clinical identifiers for early-stage primary/idiopathic adhesive capsulitis: are we seeing the real picture?
answer: The study by [PMID:24652474] was a cross-sectional study designed to validate any or all of the 8 clinical identifiers of early-stage primary/idiopathic adhesive capsulitis previously established in a Delphi study, and it included 64 patients diagnosed with early-stage adhesive capsulitis by a physical therapist or medical practitioner [PMID:24652474]. Eight active and 8 passive shoulder movements with visual analog scale pain scores for each movement were recorded before and immediately after an intra-articular injection of corticosteroid and local anesthetic; using the local anesthetic as the reference standard, pain relief of ≥70% for passive external rotation defined a positive anesthetic response (PAR), which 16 participants (25%) demonstrated [PMID:24652474]. In univariate logistic regression, three of the proposed identifiers were associated with a PAR: global loss of passive range of movement (OR=0.26, P=.03), pain at the end of range of all measured active movements (OR=0.06, P=.02), and global loss of passive glenohumeral movements (OR=0.23, P=.02) [PMID:24652474]. After stepwise removal of variables, pain at the end of range of all measured active movements remained the only identifier, but it was associated with reduced odds of a PAR [PMID:24652474]. Adhesive capsulitis is often difficult to diagnose in its early stage and to differentiate from other common shoulder disorders, and the lack of a recognized reference standard for diagnosing early-stage adhesive capsulitis remains problematic in all related research [PMID:24652474]. The diagnoses used in the related work are clinician based, as stated in [PMID:15546647], so the clinical identifiers validated in [PMID:24652474] describe an association with a local-anesthetic response among clinician-diagnosed patients rather than agreement with an established diagnostic reference standard [PMID:15546647] [PMID:24652474].

question: Is resected stomach volume related to weight loss after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy?
answer: Resected stomach volume was not significantly related to weight loss after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy: in a prospective study of 100 analyzed patients, the mean percentage excess body weight loss (%EBWL) at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months after surgery was 37.68 ± 10.97%, 50.97 ± 13.59%, 62.35 ± 11.31% and 67.59 ± 9.02% respectively, and there were no significant differences in mean %EBWL among the three groups defined by resected stomach volume (700-1,200 mL, group A, n = 21; 1,200-1,700 mL, group B, n = 62; >1,700 mL, group C, n = 17), with group means compared by analysis of variance [PMID:24827404]. The prospective study was conducted between May 2011 and April 2013, when LSG was performed in 102 consecutive patients undergoing bariatric surgery; two patients were excluded, and data from the remaining 100 patients were analyzed [PMID:24827404]. Resected stomach volume was greater in patients with higher preoperative body mass index and was positively associated with resected stomach weight [PMID:24827404].

question: Do emergency ultrasound fellowship programs impact emergency medicine residents' ultrasound education?
answer: A cross-sectional questionnaire study at 9 academic medical centers, in which 244 emergency medicine residents participated, compared ultrasound education outcomes between residency programs with and without emergency ultrasound (EUS) fellowships, with primary outcomes of number of ultrasound examinations performed, scope of bedside ultrasound applications, barriers to residents' ultrasound education, and ultrasound use in the emergency department [PMID:24866606]. Residents in programs with EUS fellowships reported performing more scans than residents in programs without fellowships (P = .04), and 30% (95% CI, 24%-35%) of the surveyed residents reported having performed more than 150 scans [PMID:24866606]. Significant differences were noted between residency programs with and without EUS fellowships in most applications of bedside ultrasound (P<.05) and in the barriers to ultrasound education (P<.05) [PMID:24866606]. As an interpretation entailed by the reported design, the cross-sectional comparison of programs with versus without EUS fellowships can document associations between fellowship presence and residents' reported ultrasound education measures but cannot establish that establishing a fellowship causes those differences; the authors also noted that no evidence previously supported EUS fellowships enhancing residents' ultrasound educational experiences [PMID:24866606].

chunks.text: Staple line leak, although rare, is among the most common postoperative complications after sleeve gastrectomy (SG) and usually occurs in the gastroesophageal (GE) junction. Increased intragastric pressure, regional ischemia, and technical failure of stapling devices have been reported as the main risk factors of postoperative leak. The aim of this study was to evaluate the impact of ischemia and intraluminal pressure in leak appearance.

Landrace swine (n = 12) were subjected to SG and total gastrectomy subsequently. Lactic acid, glycerol, and pyruvate were measured by microdialysis in GE junction and pylorus before and nine times after operation, and lactate/pyruvate (L/P) ratio was calculated as well. Moreover, ex vivo air was insufflated inside the tubularized stomach till a rupture of the staple line occurs. Maximum air pressure reached and location of rupture were recorded.

Increase of lactic acid and L/P ratio were demonstrated in GE junction measurements; however, when the measurements between GE junction and pylorus were compared, no statistically significant differences were found, with the exception of a slightly increased lactate concentration in pylorus in the midst of measurements. The maximum air pressure recorded varied from 3 to 75 mmHg (mean 24.5 mmHg) and the majority of ruptures (n = 8) occurred in GE junction. In one of them, clip displacement was noticed.

Using the GBSR, data from 5.400 LSGs were considered for analysis. Staple line leak rate decreased during the study period from 6.5 to 1.4 %. Male gender, higher BMI, concomitant sleep apnea, conversion to laparotomy, longer operation time, use of both buttresses and oversewing, and the occurrence of intraoperative complications were associated with a significantly higher leakage rate. On multivariate analysis, operation time and year of procedure only had a significant impact on staple line leak rate.

Laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) is currently being performed with increasing frequency worldwide. It offers an excellent weight loss and resolution of comorbidities in the short term with a very low incidence of complications. However, the ever present risk of a staple line leak is still a major concern.

Our series included 93 patients. Overall morbidity rate was 81 % (n = 75), with 56 % (n = 52) minor complications and 18 % (n = 17) major complications. Active smoking and excessive alcohol consumption were associated with the occurrence of severe complications, whereas BMI and low preoperative albumin levels were not. The simultaneous presence of two or more of these risk factors significantly increased the risk of postoperative complications.

Fifty-one of 2,842 patients (1.8%), ranging from 1.1% of enterectomy patients to 4.8% of total gastrectomy patients, sustained an anastomotic dehiscence. Foregut procedures were accompanied by a significantly increased rate of leakage, and depending on location, diagnosis was made between the 6th and 9th postoperative day. For each procedure, deaths from factors other than leakage far exceeded deaths from leaks. Standard risk stratifiers did not predict occurrence of leakage. Overall, 24% of patients sustaining a leak died, and this complication necessitated multiple reoperations and significantly increased length of hospital stay.

question: Does skin care frequency affect the severity of incontinence-associated dermatitis in critically ill patients?
answer: Yes — in a 9-month randomized prospective study of 99 patients, the dermatitis score on discharge in the moderate incontinence-associated dermatitis (IAD) group was significantly less in the group receiving the skin care protocol every 6 hours (7.1%) than in the group receiving it every 12 hours (10.9%; P ≤ 0.001) [PMID:25406780]. In that study, the control group received the defined skin care protocol every 12 hours and the intervention group received it every 6 hours, with both groups also receiving it as needed; the protocol consisted of cleaning with a gentle cleanser and moisturizer followed by application of a skin protectant/barrier [PMID:25406780]. The 99 patients comprised 55 in the intervention group and 44 in the control group; they were on a progressive care unit and were incontinent of urine, stool, or both, or had a fecal diversion device or urinary catheter for more than 2 days [PMID:25406780]. Dermatitis score means and P values for each group were compared using a paired t test [PMID:25406780].

chunks.text: Incontinence-associated dermatitis (IAD) is a potentially serious skin injury that can lead to pressure ulcers (PUs). Multiple studies have indicated the need for evidence to find the most effective skin care protocol to reduce the incidence and severity of IAD in critically ill patients.

To compare the incidence and severity of IAD in two groups on a progressive care unit (PCU) using a defined skin care protocol: cleaning with a gentle cleanser and moisturizer, then applying a skin protectant/barrier. The control group received the skin care protocol every 12 hours and the interventional group received the protocol every 6 hours; both groups also received it as needed.

A 9-month randomized prospective study was conducted on 99 patients (N = 55 in the intervention group and N = 44 in the control group) who were incontinent of urine, stool, or both, or had a fecal diversion device or urinary catheter for more than 2 days.

The dermatitis score in the intervention group on discharge was significantly less (7.1%; P ≤ 0.001) in the moderate IAD group than in the control group (10.9%). The dermatitis score means and P values of each group were compared using a paired t test.

To investigate what quantity of topical preparations is applied by outpatients in daily routine treatment over a 26-week period and to what extent this consumption is related to the course of the severity of patients' skin conditions.

Thirty adult outpatients (20 female and 10 male) with atopic dermatitis were examined at four different times during 26 weeks. For treatment and skin care these patients were given a topical glucocorticoid preparation (prednicarbate) and the corresponding emollient.

Newly referred patients aged>/= 14 years and with a diagnosis of either eczema or psoriasis were identified. In a randomized, parallel-group study with a follow-up period of 6 weeks, participants were randomized either to normal care, or to receive an additional session with a dermatology nurse specialist immediately after their consultation with the dermatologist. The primary outcome measure was change in quality of life at 6 weeks, as assessed by the Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI). Secondary outcomes comprised a comparison of patient knowledge at 6 weeks and the number of consultations (in secondary and primary care) that occurred during the 6-week follow-up period.

question: Should early extubation be the goal for children after congenital cardiac surgery?
answer: In a linked database analysis of all patients undergoing congenital heart surgery between July 1, 2010 and December 31, 2012, 613 children were operated on, including 97 neonates [PMID:25156467]. Intraoperative extubation was achieved in 71% of cases and early extubation within 24 hours was achieved in 89% of cases in this pediatric congenital heart surgery cohort [PMID:25156467]. Among the neonates, 63% were extubated within 24 hours, including 67% of arterial switch operations and 54% of total anomalous pulmonary venous return repairs, while Norwood operations were the only procedure in which no patient was extubated within the first 24 hours [PMID:25156467]. Multivariable logistic regression showed that the predictors of delayed extubation included preoperative mechanical ventilation, weight less than 5 kg, a longer procedure time, and the need for postoperative inotrope support [PMID:25156467]. Overall mortality in the 613 patients was 1.5% (9 of 613) [PMID:25156467]. Early extubation was associated with lower mortality (1% vs 9%, P<.001) and a lower rate of reintubation (4% vs 23%, P<.001) compared with delayed extubation [PMID:25156467]. Implementation of an early extubation strategy was associated with low rates of complications (5.1 per 10 procedures), short lengths of intensive care unit stay (median, 1 day; interquartile range, 1-3), and short hospital stays (median, 4 days; interquartile range, 3-6) [PMID:25156467]. The retrieved evidence does not establish: causal evidence that targeting early extubation improves outcomes in children after congenital cardiac surgery.

chunks.text: We sought to determine the feasibility and assess the clinical outcomes associated with an early extubation strategy for all children undergoing congenital heart surgery, including neonates (age,<30 days).

We performed a linked database analysis of all patients undergoing congenital heart surgery from July 1, 2010 to December 31, 2012. We collected data on the cardiac diagnoses, preoperative status, procedure, and postoperative course, including the duration of invasive and noninvasive ventilation, failure of extubation, hemodynamic data, length of stay, complications, and mortality. A multivariable model was used to assess the independent factors associated with an inability to extubate within the operating room and with delayed extubation (>24 hours).

We operated on 613 children, including 97 neonates. Intraoperative extubation was achieved in 71% of the cases and early extubation (≤ 24 hours) was achieved in 89% of the cases. The overall mortality was 1.5% (9 of 613 patients). Early extubation was associated with lower mortality (1% vs 9%, P<.001) and a lower rate of reintubation (4% vs 23%, P<.001) compared with delayed extubation. Notably, 63% of the neonates were extubated within 24 hours, including 67% of arterial switch operations and 54% of total anomalous pulmonary venous return repairs. Norwood operations were the only procedure in which no patient was extubated within the first 24 hours. Multivariable logistic regression demonstrated that the predictors of delayed extubation included preoperative mechanical ventilation, weight<5 kg, a longer procedure time, and the need for postoperative inotrope support. Implementation of an early extubation strategy was associated with low rates of complications (5.1 per 10 procedures), short lengths of intensive care unit stay (median, 1 day; interquartile range, 1-3), and short hospital stays (median, 4 days; interquartile range, 3-6).

Eight pediatric patients who underwent the Fontan procedure for congenital heart disease were included. Enrollment criteria were body weight>10 kg and staged Fontan procedure following the bidirectional Glenn procedure. Blood lactate concentration and central venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) were measured at five points: before skin incision, upon intensive care unit (ICU) admission, 15 minutes before, 15 minutes after, and 2 hours after extubation. Cardiac index (CI) was continuously monitored using the pulse contour technique.

We studied prospectively 87 preterm infants (mean +/- SD; birth weight: 1078 +/- 188 g; gestational age: 28.8 +/- 2.2 weeks) who were in the process of being weaned from intermittent mandatory ventilation (IMV). Infants were assigned by systematic sampling to one of the following three treatment groups: (1) direct extubation from IMV (D.EXT) (n = 30); (2) preextubation endotracheal CPAP (ET-CPAP) for 12-24 hr (n = 28); or (3) postextubation nasopharyngeal CPAP (NP-CPAP) for 12-24 hr (n = 29). Failure was defined as the need for resumption of mechanical ventilation within 72 hr of extubation due to frequent or severe apnea and/or respiratory failure (pH<7.25, PaCO2>60 mm Hg, and/or requirement for oxygen FiO2>60%).

question: Prompting Primary Care Providers about Increased Patient Risk As a Result of Family History: Does It Work?
answer: Automated, at-the-visit tailored prompts about family history risk did not significantly change problem summary list documentation of risk status or screening interventions for any of the 6 diseases (heart disease, stroke, diabetes, and breast, colorectal or ovarian cancer), although physicians did document a response to most prompts [PMID:25957366]. The 492 eligible primary care patients (aged 35-65 with moderate or strong familial risk) made 847 visits during the study period, of which 152 visits had no documentation of a response to a family history prompt [PMID:25957366]. Among the remaining 695 visits, physician responses were: reviewed family history (n = 372, 53.5%), discussed family history (n = 159, 22.9%), not addressed (n = 155, 22.3%), and reviewed family history and ordered tests/referrals (n = 5, 0.7%) [PMID:25957366]. Because the main outcome measures were PCP response to the prompts, addition of family history risk to problem summary lists, and patient screening status, the reported results concern documentation and screening behaviour rather than demonstrated clinical outcomes [PMID:25957366].

chunks.text: Electronic health records have the potential to facilitate family history use by primary care physicians (PCPs) to provide personalized care. The objective of this study was to determine whether automated, at-the-visit tailored prompts about family history risk change PCP behavior.

Automated, tailored prompts highlighting familial risk for heart disease, stroke, diabetes, and breast, colorectal, or ovarian cancer were implemented during 2011 to 2012. Medical records of a cohort of community-based primary care patients, aged 35 to 65 years, who previously participated in our Family Healthware study and had a moderate or strong familial risk for any of the 6 diseases were subsequently reviewed. The main outcome measures were PCP response to the prompts, adding family history risk to problem summary lists, and patient screening status for each disease.

The 492 eligible patients had 847 visits during the study period; 152 visits had no documentation of response to a family history prompt. Of the remaining 695 visits, physician responses were reviewed family history (n = 372, 53.5%), discussed family history (n = 159, 22.9%), not addressed (n = 155, 22.3%), and reviewed family history and ordered tests/referrals (n = 5, 0.7%). There was no significant change in problem summary list documentation of risk status or screening interventions for any of the 6 diseases.
